newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's central bank may tighten while in easing mode.
newsitem.headline: NZ's central bank may tighten while in easing mode.

text.p: New Zealand's central bank may have to tighten monetary conditions while in a major easing mode, analysts said on Friday.
Confused? Well, so are plenty others.
Dealers say the Reserve Bank of New Zealand may be boxed into a corner and its respected credibility is on the line.
Last Friday it sanctioned a 100 basis point easing in its Monetary Policy Statement and said, provided things panned out, it would allow another 40 point easing in the December quarter.
It also said it would tolerate the market moving 50 basis points either side of a desired level -- 825 in the September quarter on its Monetary Conditions Index (MCI) NZ/MCI.
Unsurprisingly, the market took the 100 points for the September quarter, plus the December quarter, and then some.
The index was at 750 on Thursday when bank Governor Don Brash issued a warning to markets, saying conditions were too easy and the bank wanted them settling nearer desired levels.
But the market didn't really heed the warning and the index ended on Thursday at at 763, 12 points below the desired level.
"They are suffering a serious credibility problem," said ANZ Bank senior manager of domestic markets, Jim Reardon.
"They seem ineffectual having come out a week ago and said the band was at 50, they already seem to be tolerating 60.
"If they are going to say 50, they have to defend 50. They can't say 50 and defend 70.
"Right from they outset they need to decide where their tolerance barriers are and act," Reardon added.
The options for the bank are seen as limited.

It can make a second attempt at jawboning, risking the market again ignoring it and further damaging its credibility, or it could wield its big stick and lower the daily cash target -- a formal tightening.
The trouble with that is the economy has been losing momentum, with GDP falling 0.5 percent in the March quarter, and such a move would be likely to put the brakes on altogether.
"The next move is a very aggressive statement and if that doesn't work, they can come in and remove some cash from the system," said Bankers Trust New Zealand Deputy Chief Executive John MacFarlane.
But he thought the market would test the bank again shortly.
"The market is a beast that likes to test to boundaries, that's its nature. It's not the RB painting themselves into a corner, it's the market's desire to always test the boundaries."

WestpacTrust economist Joselyn Stroombergen said the consequences of a reduction in the cash target at this stage of the cycle would be very negative, even though Brash said on Wednesday that the economy picked up in the June quarter.
She said that if the economy was still slowing and the RB hiked interest rates it would drive the economy into the wall.
"It's way too early to talk about raising interest rates," she said. "We are in a very uncertain phase."
But Stroombergen did not believe the bank was on the point of raising the cash target.
"It's still a long way off, unless interest rates fall below seven percent," she said. Short rates on the key 90-day bank bills remained at around 7.16 percent on Friday.
She argued that although the MCI did not move much after the RB's warning on Thursday, the mix of conditions altered to the RB's liking -- a softer currency and higher short rates.
"The RB is trying to buy itself breathing space until it becomes clear whether its more optimistic view of the economy or the market's (view) is revealed as correct," she said.
